newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crudes down sharply, grades extend weakness.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crudes down sharply, grades extend weakness.

text.p: U.S. crudes experienced sharp losses Monday, pushed lower by late headlines saying the U.S. has asked Saudi Arabia to produce more oil to replace delayed Iraqi exports under the U.N. oil-for-food accord.
The U.S. government quickly shot down the story, as did sources in the Middle East.
Outright cash prices declined in line with the futures selling, ending around $23.25-$23.35 for October West Texas Intermediate/Cushing, off more than $1.00 from Friday.
Crudes were pressured from the morning by the easing of tensions over the weekend between the U.S. and Iraq.

Domestic grades were dull and stuck in weaker trading ranges, with only sporadic deals seen for Texas and Lousiana parcels. Most players said the drastic price fluctuations in the outright market kept players on the sidelines.
North Sea imports have pressured domestic grades in recent sessions, leaving refiners to dump holdings, traders said.
Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James was talked all session at 25-30 cts over WTI/Cushing, with last trades at plus 27 cts.
Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire recouped some of its value by day's end, talked at a 6-12 cts premium to the WTI, after spending most Friday and early Monday around flat.
WTI/Cushing Posting Plus fell 20-30 cts, trading at $2.10 from deals Friday above $2.30. The weakening of the Oct/Nov spread played into the retreat, traders said.
Sour grades were talked at minus $1.20-$1.16 for West Texas Sour/Midland, and Eugene Island was steady at minus $1.12-$1.09, with last deals at a $1.10 discount to WTI/Cushing.

Brent paper deals were done for Nov Brent at slightly weaker levels in the U.S. aftermarket. Traders confirmed there were partial deals from $21.48-$21.55, down 7 cts to even with the IPE Nov Brent settlement at $21.55.
Spreads were also exchanged, with Oct/Nov Brent sold at 43 cts, 44 cts and 45 cts, down some 20 cts from earlier Monday.
A Nov/Dec Brent spread was sold at 50 cts, traders noted.
The outright price collapse and narrow arbitrage between WTI and Brent has kept most North Sea business quiet to the U.S. Gulf.
